clinicalPearls: Infertility is defined as failure to conceive after 12 months of unprotected intercourse; global prevalence is roughly 17.5%, affecting an estimated 48-72 million couples (Harrison 22e p.3149).

Primary infertility describes couples who have never conceived, whereas secondary infertility follows at least one prior pregnancy; about 85% of couples conceive within 12 months and 95% within 24 months (Harrison 22e p.3149).

Female-only factors account for roughly 30-40% of cases, male-only factors 40-50%, combined factors 20-30%, and unexplained infertility up to about 30% - so a complete workup of BOTH partners is recommended (Harrison 22e p.3149-3150).

Fecundability falls steeply with maternal age: compared with women aged 30-31, it is reduced about 14% at 34-35, 53% at 40-41, and 59% at 42-44 years, largely from oocyte meiotic chromosomal errors; a comparable decline is NOT seen in men under 50 (Harrison 22e p.3149).
Evaluation is generally started after 12 months of trying, but after only 6 months if the female partner is over 35 and immediately if she is over 40 (Harrison 22e p.3150).

The fertile window is about 5-6 days before ovulation; intercourse every 1-2 days during this interval maximizes the chance of conception. A basal body temperature rise confirms ovulation has already occurred and therefore cannot be used prospectively to time intercourse (Harrison 22e p.3151).

Long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARC; IUDs and subdermal implants) are the most effective reversible methods, rivaling sterilization, with high continuation and satisfaction rates, making them a good choice even for adolescents and nulliparous women (Harrison 22e p.3153-3154).

Combined estrogen-progestin contraceptives reduce the risk of endometrial cancer (about 50%) and ovarian cancer (about 40%) and help regulate cycles and reduce menorrhagia, dysmenorrhea and hyperandrogenism (Harrison 22e p.3153).

Unintended pregnancies arise mainly from non-use or inconsistent use rather than method failure; methods requiring daily or coitus-related use fail more often than LARC and permanent methods (Harrison 22e p.3152-3153).

Emergency contraception should be offered to any woman who requests it up to 5 days after unprotected intercourse and should NOT be delayed for a pregnancy test or exam; the copper IUD is the most effective option and ulipristal acetate the most effective oral agent (Harrison 22e p.3154).

Lactation can provide effective contraception during the first 6 postpartum months only if breastfeeding is exclusive and menses have not resumed, with failure rates as low as 0.5-1.5 per 100 women-years (Harrison 22e p.3154).
harrison.pathophysiology: Conception requires ovulation of a competent oocyte, patent fallopian tubes, a receptive uterus, and adequate sperm delivery and function; disruption at any step causes infertility. Female causes include tubal damage (often from pelvic inflammatory disease, endometriosis, prior surgery, or salpingitis isthmica nodosum), uterine factors (fibroids distorting the cavity, congenital mullerian anomalies, intrauterine scarring), ovulatory dysfunction (PCOS, diminished ovarian reserve, premature ovarian insufficiency), and endocrine disturbance (hypothyroidism, hyperprolactinemia). Age-related decline reflects accumulating meiotic chromosomal errors in the oocyte after 35. Male causes include anatomic/obstructive problems (vasectomy, infection, congenital absence of the vas), endocrine causes (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, hyperprolactinemia, morbid obesity, certain drugs and exogenous testosterone suppressing spermatogenesis), sexual dysfunction, and primary testicular/genetic defects (Klinefelter syndrome, Y-chromosome microdeletions). Hormonal contraception works through negative feedback: continuous estrogen suppresses FSH and follicular development while continuous progestin suppresses the LH surge and ovulation, thickens cervical mucus, thins/alters the endometrium, and impairs tubal motility; progestin-only and levonorgestrel-IUD effects rely mainly on cervical mucus thickening and endometrial thinning. Copper IUDs act as a spermicide that also impairs fertilization and implantation (Harrison 22e p.3149-3154).
additionalDifferentials: Polycystic ovary syndrome (most common cause of anovulatory infertility)
Diminished ovarian reserve / premature ovarian insufficiency
Hypothalamic amenorrhea (low body weight, excessive exercise)
Hyperprolactinemia and thyroid dysfunction causing anovulation
Uterine fibroids/polyps/intrauterine adhesions distorting the cavity
infectionMimics: Tubal factor infertility secondary to sexually transmitted infection-related salpingitis (the infection causes structural damage; chronic infertility itself is non-infective)
Mumps orchitis as a historical cause of testicular damage and male infertility
nonInfectiousMimics: Endometriosis presenting with pelvic pain and dysmenorrhea overlapping other gynecologic disease
Fibroid-related symptoms mimicking other uterine pathology
Anovulation from systemic endocrine disease (thyroid, prolactin)
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal and abdominal pelvic ultrasound for uterine/adnexal pathology and antral follicle count (ovarian reserve)
Ovulation assessment: urinary LH detection kits or serum progesterone ~7 days after ovulation
Hysterosalpingogram (HSG) or saline infusion sonogram to assess tubal patency and intrauterine pathology
Ovarian reserve testing: day 2-3 serum FSH and estradiol plus anti-mullerian hormone (AMH) and antral follicle counts
Endocrine tests in irregular menses: serum TSH, prolactin, total and free testosterone
Semen analysis after 2-7 days abstinence (count, motility, morphology, volume, pH); WHO oligoasthenozoospermia thresholds: sperm count <15 million/mL, motility <40%, normal morphology <4%
Genetic evaluation (karyotype and Y-chromosome microdeletion) for azoospermia or severe oligospermia (<5 million/mL); CFTR testing in congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
Preconception genetic carrier screening based on ethnicity/family history
redFlags: Female partner over 40 years - evaluate immediately rather than waiting
Azoospermia or severe oligospermia (<5 million/mL) - requires genetic and endocrine evaluation
Smoker aged 35 or older using >=15 cigarettes/day - USMEC category 4 contraindication to estrogen-containing contraception
History of venous thromboembolism, known thrombogenic mutations, stroke, or ischemic heart disease - avoid estrogen-containing contraceptives
Migraine with aura - contraindication to combined hormonal contraception
Current breast cancer - contraindication to hormonal contraception
Recurrent pregnancy loss - consider sperm DNA fragmentation assay
harrison.prognosis: About 85% of couples not using contraception conceive within one year and 95% within two years, but success of fertility treatment depends strongly on the female partner's age, ovarian reserve, smoking, BMI, and race; advanced maternal age (>35) raises aneuploidy risk and advanced paternal age (>40) is linked to adverse offspring outcomes. IVF carries an overall low complication risk, with multiple pregnancy being the main hazard and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome reduced by careful monitoring and GnRH (rather than hCG) triggering. Infertility causes substantial psychological stress, but the condition and its treatment do not appear to produce long-term psychological sequelae (Harrison 22e p.3149-3152).
pitfalls: Treating only one partner - both must be evaluated because male, female, and combined factors are common.
Using basal body temperature to time intercourse prospectively; the temperature rise only confirms ovulation has already happened.
Over-relying on HSG positive findings - its positive predictive value for tubal occlusion is low even though its negative predictive value is high.

Performing routine sperm-antibody testing, scrotal ultrasound, diagnostic laparoscopy, postcoital test, endometrial biopsy, thrombophilia, immunologic testing, or karyotype as part of the initial infertility workup - these are NOT indicated routinely.
Attempting tubal repair/reconstruction with hydrosalpinx or prior tubal infection - low success and increased ectopic risk; salpingectomy of hydrosalpinges actually improves subsequent IVF outcomes.
Routine screening for familial thrombotic disorders before prescribing hormonal contraception is not recommended.
Withholding or delaying emergency contraception to obtain a pregnancy test or exam, or withholding it from overweight/obese women.
Assuming individual abnormal semen parameters predict infertility - none alone is predictive; risk rises with multiple abnormalities.
harrison.severityClassification: Contraceptive choice is guided by the U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria (USMEC, adapted from WHO): Category 4 = unacceptable health risk (e.g., smoker >=35 years with >=15 cigarettes/day, acute DVT or prior VTE at high recurrence risk, stroke or thrombogenic mutations, complicated valvular disease, current breast cancer, migraine with aura, uncontrolled hypertension >=160/100); Category 3 = theoretical/proven risks outweigh benefits (e.g., smoker >=35 with <15 cigarettes/day, controlled or moderate hypertension, certain enzyme-inducing anticonvulsants, rifampin/rifabutin, some HIV regimens, bariatric malabsorptive surgery); Category 2 = benefits generally outweigh risks (e.g., obesity alone). Method effectiveness ranges from highly effective sterilization and LARC (>99%) to less reliable barrier and fertility-awareness methods (Harrison 22e p.3152-3153).
